entries.title: What decides a case is whether the works needed ground people were living on
entries.conviction: Reached independently by three batches of research in one round. Not yet tested against a queue in advance.
entries.summary:
Two things that look as though they should predict where lending did harm do not. Region does not: a round that deliberately put African, South Asian and South-East Asian projects first produced 18 cases and not one of them had a source outside the lender. Sector does not either: a round split 36 projects between the sectors where earlier cases had survived and the sectors where earlier drops had clustered, and the supposedly barren half returned 10 cases from 18 projects while the productive road half returned 5 from 11. Five of eighteen projects in one batch were filed under a sector their own documents contradict; one called a water project is a 296.5 km high-voltage transmission line, coded entirely to transmission and distribution, and carries the water tag only because the words Nile Basin Initiative are in its name.

What the three batches each arrived at separately is physical. River embankments, urban drainage, a landfill buffer zone, a dam reservoir, a riverfront, a transmission line and a road through a town produced cases. Village wells and latrines, on-farm water saving, canal rehabilitation, subsurface drainage and sector-wide programme support did not. The difference is whether the works needed a construction site that somebody was living or trading on.

The lenders say it themselves, in the projects' own resettlement plans, before any work begins. Five projects that produced no case carry a sentence of this kind: 'No physical relocation of households is required', which one Georgian project states twice; 'No loss of primary and secondary structures and no relocation of households' in Kiribati; 'No displacement / Resettlement is required' in Rajasthan; 'there will be no relocation of people' at Ma'anshan, whose completion report later reuses that clause with the second half removed; and 'none of the project affected people will be severely affected or require relocation' in Vietnam. A sixth states it as an outcome rather than a plan.
entries.implications: If it holds, the queue can be screened before any research is done, from one sentence in a document the lender publishes at appraisal. That would cut the reading on projects that cannot produce a case and leave the time for the ones that can. It also means the sector and country labels on a lead list are close to useless for this purpose, and that a project's size tells you less than what its works physically required.
entries.missing: It has only ever been noticed after the fact, on projects already researched. Nobody has applied it to a queue in advance and then checked whether it was right. Its limit is already known: a project with a framework plus fifteen subproject plans has no single sentence to search, so the screen narrows a queue rather than filtering it.
entries.would_settle: Apply the sentence as a screen to the projects still on the queue before researching any of them. Write down which ones it predicts will produce nothing. Then research them anyway and compare.

story: Here is something a lender writes down before it hands over any money, and that nobody outside uses. Buried in the resettlement plan of a project at the appraisal stage is a sentence saying whether the works will need ground that people are living or trading on. That single sentence appears to predict whether a project will hurt anyone better than its sector, its country or its size do. If that is right, harm of this kind is foreseeable in advance, in public, by anyone who reads the plan.

The way this surfaced is worth knowing, because it was not what anyone was looking for. One round of research deliberately put African, South Asian and South-East Asian projects first, on the assumption that region would predict where lending did damage. It produced 18 cases and not one of them had a source outside the lender's own documents. Another round split 36 projects between the sectors where earlier cases had survived and the sectors where earlier attempts had failed; the supposedly barren half returned 10 cases from 18 projects while the promising road half returned 5 from 11. Sector labels turned out to be unreliable in a plainer way too: five of eighteen projects in one batch were filed under a sector their own documents contradict. One listed as a water project is a 296.5 km high-voltage transmission line, with all of the lender's money coded to transmission and distribution. It carries the water tag because the words Nile Basin Initiative are in its name.

What did predict the cases was physical. River embankments, urban drainage, a landfill buffer zone, a dam reservoir, a riverfront, a transmission line and a road driven through a town all produced them. Village wells and latrines, on-farm water saving, canal rehabilitation, subsurface drainage and sector-wide programme support produced none. The dividing line is whether the work needed a construction site that somebody was already on. And the lenders state it themselves, in advance: a Georgian project's plan says no physical relocation of households is required, and says it twice; a Kiribati plan rules out any loss of structures or relocation; a Rajasthan plan says no displacement is required; a Vietnamese plan says nobody affected will be severely affected or need to move. None of those projects produced a case. At Ma'anshan in China the plan says there will be no relocation of people, and the completion report reuses the clause with its second half cut off.

The reason this is a suspicion is that it has only ever been noticed afterwards, on projects already researched. Nobody has taken the projects still waiting in the queue, read that one sentence, written down which ones it predicts will produce nothing, and then researched them anyway to see whether the prediction held. That is the whole test, and it costs nothing but order of work. Its limit is already known: a project with an overall framework plus fifteen separate subproject plans has no single sentence to search, so the screen narrows a queue rather than filtering it.

entries.title: What the evaluators leave out of their own reports runs one way
entries.conviction: Five document pairs read closely, every one pointing the same direction. Five pairs is not a count.
entries.summary:
Most of the cases on this map rest on the lender's own documents. Of the 430 cases involving the World Bank or the IFC, 199 are marked disputed for that reason: searches for press reporting, field research, court records and complaints found nothing outside the lender for them. So what the lender's documents leave out is not a detail about one project. It decides what this map can know.

Two documents describe each project. The lender's staff write a completion report when the money runs out, and the Independent Evaluation Group writes a review of that report. The reviews have been found dropping what the reports record, and citing the paragraph they leave out. One review omits ten fatalities, blasting carried out without permits, and 183 outstanding compensation cases. A second quotes a report up to the sentence before a fatality and stops. A third turns 249 families, and sites handed to a contractor before anyone was paid, into the sentence 'All Project Affected Families were eventually compensated'.

The gap can be large even on a plain number. On a Philippine national roads project the completion report's own indicator table gives roads in good or fair condition at 55 per cent, marked 'No change from baseline', against a revised target of 60. The review of that report gives 77 per cent, says the project exceeded its target, and attributes the figure to the project team rather than to any document. Neither paper explains the difference.

A separate audit of 46 cases found 19 carrying a factual error in the field that describes the lender's role, and three classes of that error came from reading a figure or a rating out of the review's summary table instead of out of the report the table summarises.
entries.implications: If the omissions run one way, then the harm recorded on this map is a floor and not a measure, and any figure taken from a review alone is low. It would also mean the evaluation reviews cannot be used as a check on the reports, which is how they are usually read, and that a card citing a rating must name which of the two documents gave it.
entries.missing: Five pairs, every one found by a checker sent to look at something else. No systematic comparison has been run, so there is no count of how often the reviews omit, in which direction, or whether some reviewers do it and others do not. The documents for 46 of the 95 cases drawn from the ICIJ list have been read closely; the other 49 have not been audited at all.
entries.would_settle: Read every paired completion report and evaluation review on the map, count the omissions, and record which direction each one runs. One-directional omissions across a hundred pairs would settle it.

entries.title: The body that took the land is usually an arm of the state, not a company
entries.conviction: Two counted samples, both lopsided the same way, both from the same kind of document.
entries.summary:
This map was built around money from abroad and the companies that came with it, and it carries a field on every card for the companies that took part. On the cases drawn from the lenders' own completion reports, that field is filling up with governments.

Of 27 new names added by one round of research, 25 were state bodies: project management offices, provincial transport departments, national roads agencies, municipal corporations and a State Council poverty reduction office. In an earlier round a checker found that on four of eight cards in one batch the companies list held ministries, city governments and state institutes, and that no contractor was named on any of the eight. The reason is in the source: a completion report names the agency that carried out the project and almost never names the firm that did the work.

The map now holds 1,177 distinct company names across 1,093 cases, and none of them has been sorted into state bodies, private firms and special-purpose vehicles. Two narrower versions of the same problem have already been fixed on individual cards. A civil society oversight body set up under a project's own anti-corruption measures was removed from a Philippine card, where listing it beside the department that allowed uncompensated works read as an accusation no document makes. And a Kazakh roads company was rewritten after a completion report showed it was an output of the loan, created in 2013 at the lender's own recommendation, rather than a body that had implemented anything.
entries.implications: A reader opening Companies to see which firms were involved finds a roads committee. If the count holds across the map, the field is describing the state carrying out lender-financed works, and either it needs splitting or the cards need to say plainly that the body named is a government agency. Splitting it means a migration across 1,093 cases and a new section on every card, and that cost grows with every round of research.
entries.missing: Nobody has classified the 1,177 names. Both samples come from projects drawn from one list of one lender's documents, so the lopsidedness may belong to that material rather than to the map. Private lending, foreign company investment and Chinese state money would have to be counted separately before this could be called general.
entries.would_settle: Sort all 1,177 names into state bodies, private firms, special-purpose vehicles and others, and count them against the kind of money that paid for each case. The names are already in the data and the work needs no new sources.

story: This map was built around money coming in from outside and the companies that arrive with it, and every card has a field for the companies involved. On the cases that come from the lenders' own completion reports, that field is filling up with governments. The probable position is that when foreign money pays for works and somebody loses their home to them, the body that actually takes the ground is usually an arm of their own state — a project management office, a provincial transport department, a municipal corporation — and not the foreign firm anyone would think to blame.

One round of research added 27 new names to the map and 25 of them were state bodies: project offices, provincial transport departments, national roads agencies, municipal corporations, a State Council poverty reduction office. An earlier round found that on four of eight cards in a single batch the companies list held ministries, city governments and state institutes, and that no contractor was named on any of the eight. The reason is in the source document. A completion report names the agency that carried out the project. It almost never names the firm that did the digging.

Nobody has sorted the names, and that is the gap. The map holds 1,177 distinct company names across 1,093 cases, and not one of them has been classified as a state body, a private firm or a special-purpose vehicle. Both samples also come from projects drawn from one list of one lender's documents, so the lopsidedness may belong to that material rather than to the world: private lending, foreign company investment and Chinese state money would each have to be counted separately before this could be called general.

Getting it wrong in either direction does damage, which is why two cards have already been corrected. A civil society oversight body was taken off a Philippine card after it turned out to exist under the project's own anti-corruption measures; listing it beside the department that had allowed uncompensated works read as an accusation no document supports. Meanwhile a reader opening Companies to see which firms were involved can find a roads committee. Sorting all 1,177 names against the kind of money that paid for each case needs no new sources, because the names are already in the data.

entries.title: The works came first and the payment after
entries.conviction: Five cases with the same sequence, none of them sought. Twenty cards mention valuation below replacement cost, which may be the commoner failure.
entries.summary:
Where a lender's resettlement policy is broken on the cases here, the break is often not in the amount offered but in the order of events: the ground is taken, the works are built, and the money arrives later or not at all.

On a Ugandan rural electrification grid the works were finished before compensation was paid, and payments were completed six months after the loan had closed. On the Kawanda to Masaka transmission line the utility used an interim court order and armed police to force the works through at Galatiya over occupants who had not been paid, then energized the line on 1 June 2018 with people still living beneath it; the lender's own report calls both of those breaches of its resettlement policy. A completion report elsewhere records 249 families, and sites handed to the contractor before payment, which the review of that report compresses into 'All Project Affected Families were eventually compensated'. At the Peshawar landfill 99 acres were taken in 2017 under the urgency clause of the Land Acquisition Act, 85 of 234 landowners were still unpaid in April 2023, the valuation came in 31.43 per cent below replacement cost, and open dumping began as soon as possession was taken. At Bukoba airport compensation was unpaid in five identified resettlement cases at a named site.

Against that, twenty cards on this map mention compensation below replacement cost, which is the other way a resettlement fails. Nobody has counted which of the two is commoner.
entries.implications: If the sequence is the usual failure, then what breaks a safeguard policy is a works schedule rather than a valuation, and the thing to look for in a document is a pair of dates rather than a figure. It would also mean a project can satisfy every requirement on paper and still take land by force, because the policy is met at the end and broken in the middle.
entries.missing: Five cases, none of them looked for. No case on the map has been coded for the two dates that would show the sequence: when works began on the ground, and when compensation was paid. The twenty replacement-cost mentions have not been counted properly either, so the comparison that matters has not been made.
entries.would_settle: Code every case drawn from the ICIJ list for those two dates. The completion reports carry both often enough to count, and the result would show which of the two failures is commoner.

countries.note: On the Kawanda-Masaka line the utility used an interim court order and armed police at Galatiya and energized the line on 1 June 2018 with people still beneath it. On a rural electrification grid the works finished before compensation was paid and payments completed six months after closing.

story: Every large lender has a resettlement policy, and it promises that people losing land or homes are compensated. On the cases here the promise is usually kept in the end. What goes wrong is the order. The ground is taken, the works are built, and the money arrives afterwards or not at all — which means a project can satisfy every requirement on paper while the people on that land are moved off it by force.

The clearest sequence on this map is Ugandan. On the Kawanda to Masaka transmission line the utility used an interim court order and armed police to push the works through at Galatiya, over occupants who had not been paid, and then energised the line on 1 June 2018 with people still living underneath it. The lender's own report calls both of those breaches of its resettlement policy. On a separate Ugandan rural electrification grid the works were finished before compensation was paid, and the payments were only completed six months after the loan had closed. At the Peshawar landfill in Pakistan, 99 acres were taken in 2017 under the urgency clause of the Land Acquisition Act; 85 of the 234 landowners were still unpaid in April 2023, the valuation came in 31.43 per cent below replacement cost, and open dumping started as soon as possession was taken. At Bukoba airport in Tanzania compensation was unpaid in five identified resettlement cases.

If this is the usual way a safeguard fails, then what breaks it is a construction schedule rather than a valuation, and the thing to look for in a project document is a pair of dates rather than a figure — when the machines arrived, and when the money did.

Set against that, twenty cards on this map mention compensation paid below replacement cost, which is the other way these policies fail, and nobody has counted which of the two is commoner. The five cases here were not sought; each was noticed while a round of research was doing something else. No case on this map has been coded for those two dates, and the twenty replacement-cost mentions have not been properly counted either, so the comparison that matters has not been made. The completion reports carry both dates often enough to count, which makes this one of the cheaper things on the queue to settle.

entries.title: Compensation paid into a court the owner never reaches
entries.conviction: Four cards, three of them in one country. A documented mechanism, too few cases to call it usual.
entries.summary:
There is a way for a project to record compensation as paid while the owner gets nothing. The money is deposited with a court, possession is taken, and whether anyone ever collects is a separate matter that the project's own records do not follow.

On the Orissa state roads project 7,948 people were enumerated, 1,890 of them ruled ineligible under the project's own policy, and 1,376 of 7,698 land awards were unpaid, with money paid into court deposits because the owners never collected it. Borrower performance was rated unsatisfactory and the lender suspended disbursements for 17 months. On the second Karnataka state highways project, compliance with the resettlement policy was rated unsatisfactory for over three years, over 40 per cent of compensation was deposited with the courts, income tax was deducted from landowners against the project's own policy, 1,778 complaints were filed, and two named villages were still unresettled in 2019. Two further cards carry the same mechanism: a bus corridor in India, and the Tilenga oilfield and East African crude oil pipeline land acquisition in Uganda.

Three of the four are Indian state road projects, which is either where the mechanism is used or where this map happens to have looked.
entries.implications: A deposit turns an unpaid owner into a completed line in a project's accounts. If it is routine in Indian land acquisition, then every Indian road case on this map needs its compensation figures read as deposits rather than payments, and so does every lender report that calls compensation disbursed.
entries.missing: Four cards. They were found by searching the text of all 1,093 cards, which finds only cases whose text already says it, so four is a floor and not a count. Nobody has read the deposit provision in either country's land acquisition statute, and nobody has checked the court records to see whether the deposits were collected.
entries.would_settle: Read the deposit provision in the land acquisition statute of each country where it appears, then look for a deposit figure in every Indian road and corridor case on this map. If most carry one, the deposit is how the system works rather than one project's failure.

countries.role: Three cases, two of them state road projects
countries.note: Orissa: 1,376 of 7,698 land awards unpaid, money in court deposits because owners never collected, disbursements suspended for 17 months. Karnataka: over 40 per cent of compensation deposited with the courts, income tax wrongly deducted, 1,778 complaints, two villages still unresettled in 2019. A third case is a bus corridor.

story: There is a lawful way for a project to record compensation as paid while the owner of the land receives nothing. The money is deposited with a court, possession of the land is taken, and whether anyone ever collects it is a separate question that the project's own records do not follow. On a lender's books, and in its reports, the compensation has been disbursed.

The Orissa state roads project shows the whole mechanism. Of the people enumerated, 7,948 in all, 1,890 were ruled ineligible under the project's own policy, and 1,376 of 7,698 land awards went unpaid, the money sitting in court deposits because the owners never collected it. Borrower performance was rated unsatisfactory and the lender suspended disbursements for 17 months. On the second Karnataka state highways project, compliance with the resettlement policy was rated unsatisfactory for over three years, more than 40 per cent of the compensation was deposited with the courts, income tax was deducted from landowners against the project's own policy, 1,778 complaints were filed, and two named villages were still unresettled in 2019. Two further cards carry the same mechanism: a bus corridor in India, and the Tilenga oilfield and East African crude oil pipeline land acquisition in Uganda.

The practical consequence for anyone reading a lender's report is direct. A line saying compensation was disbursed may describe money lodged with a court, and if the mechanism is routine in Indian land acquisition rather than one project's failure, then the compensation figures on every Indian road case here have to be read that way too.

Four cards is not a count. They were found by searching the text of every card on this map, which only finds cases whose own text already says the thing, so four is a floor. Three of the four are Indian state road projects, which is either where the mechanism is used or simply where this map has happened to look. Two documents would settle it, and neither is hard to get: the deposit provision in the land acquisition statute of each country where it appears, and then a check for a deposit figure in every Indian road and corridor case here. Court records would show the other half — whether the deposits were ever collected, or whether these are ordinary escrow arrangements over disputed title that owners did claim in the end.

entries.title: The empty regions mark a missing register, not an absence of harm
entries.conviction: Consistent with how every part of this map was built, and not yet set against how much money each country actually took.
entries.summary:
This map holds 1,093 cases in 129 countries, and the thinnest parts of it are the Middle East and North Africa, and Europe and Central Asia. There is a straightforward explanation for the shape that has nothing to do with where harm happened.

Six rounds of research added 101 cases and exactly one new country. Every other case fell in a country already on the map. All six worked a single list, built by journalists who read one lender's documents for one decade, and that list covers 124 countries. A region it never reached stays empty however much work is done on it.

The same holds by kind of money rather than by place. Where a register exists the coverage is reasonable: all 3,001 complaints published by fourteen complaint offices have been read, and 434 of the 483 that record harm on the ground sit inside a case. Where no register exists the coverage collapses: 9 cases against the 20,032 foreign company projects UNCTAD counted for 2021 to 2023, 4 against 1,332 investor-state lawsuits, 82 against AidData's 20,985 Chinese state loans, and 35 against 1.5 million recorded aid activities. Nobody publishes a list of the loans, grants and investments that harmed people, so for most kinds of money there is nothing to divide by.
entries.implications: If the shape of the map tracks where registers exist, then a reader cannot take an empty region as a quiet one, and the map should say so where the emptiness shows. It would also mean that building coverage in those regions is not a research problem but a sourcing problem: there is no list to work from, and no amount of reading the lenders' documents produces one.
entries.missing: The comparison that would show it has not been made. Per-country case counts have never been set against how much lending and investment each country actually received, although the map already carries the World Development Indicators and the International Debt Statistics.
entries.would_settle: Divide each country's case count by its lending and investment over the same years. If the thin countries borrowed heavily, the gap is in the record rather than in the world.
entries.looked_at: The country counts and the lending totals are both on this map already. Nobody has divided one by the other.
story: Look at this map and parts of the world are nearly empty: the Middle East and North Africa, and Europe and Central Asia. The temptation is to read that as quiet. The probable explanation has nothing to do with where harm happened. It is that somebody keeps a list in some places and nobody keeps one in others, and this map can only hold what somebody wrote down.

The evidence is in how the map was built. Six rounds of research added 101 cases and exactly one country that was not already on it. Every other case landed in a country the map already held. All six rounds worked the same list, compiled by journalists who read one lender's documents for one decade, and that list reaches 124 countries. A region it never covered stays blank however much work is done.

The same split shows up by kind of money rather than by place, and the contrast is stark. Where a register exists, coverage is good: every one of the 3,001 complaints published by fourteen complaint offices has been read, and 434 of the 483 that record harm on the ground now sit inside a case on this map. Where no register exists, it collapses. There are 9 cases here against the 20,032 foreign company projects UNCTAD counted for 2021 to 2023; 4 against 1,332 investor-state lawsuits; 82 against AidData's 20,985 Chinese state loans; and 35 against 1.5 million recorded aid activities. Nobody anywhere publishes a list of the loans, grants and investments that hurt people, so for most kinds of money there is no denominator to work from and nothing to search.

What follows for a reader is simple and worth stating plainly: white space on this map is not evidence of safety. It is evidence that no register exists. It also means building coverage in those regions is not a research problem that more reading will solve, because there is no list to read. The comparison that would confirm it has not been made, and the data for it is already here — the map carries the World Development Indicators and the International Debt Statistics, so each country's case count can be divided by the lending and investment it actually received over the same years. If the thin countries borrowed heavily, the gap is in the record rather than in the world.

entries.title: The conditions on a loan follow the largest members' voting power as well as the borrower's numbers
entries.conviction: Two published studies and the two lenders' own voting tables. One study is a journal article, the other a 2003 working paper. Nothing on this map's own cases has been matched against either.
entries.summary:
Both main lenders give their members votes in proportion to what they have paid in, so the members are not equal. The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development's own table of subscriptions and voting power, data as of 30 June 2026, gives 2,918,202 votes across 189 countries. The United States holds 466,319 of them, 15.98 per cent. Japan holds 6.88 per cent, China 5.75 per cent, Germany 4.09 per cent, France and the United Kingdom 3.75 per cent each. The IMF's Annual Report 2025 gives the same shape for the Fund as of 30 April 2025: the United States casts 831,394 votes, 16.49 per cent of the total, Japan 6.14 per cent and China 6.08 per cent.

Those percentages meet thresholds written into the IMF's Articles of Agreement. The index to the Articles gathers under one heading the decisions that need an eighty-five per cent majority of the total voting power; counted for this entry, that heading carries 22 entries, among them adjustment of quotas, establishment of the Council, the number of Executive Directors and compulsory withdrawal of a member. Article XXVIII(a) says that an amendment takes effect when "three-fifths of the members, having eighty-five percent of the total voting power, have accepted" it. Eighty-five per cent of the votes cannot be assembled without a member that holds more than 15 per cent of them, because 100 minus 85 is 15.

What gets attached to a loan has been counted twice. Kentikelenis, Stubbs and King, in the Review of International Political Economy, searched 4,590 loan-related documents for 1985 to 2014 and extracted 55,465 individual conditions across 131 countries; the median number of conditions applicable per year was about 42 over 1996 to 2007 and 44 in 2014. Dreher and Jensen, in a 2003 working paper, read 206 letters of intent from 38 countries signed between April 1997 and February 2003 and set the number of conditions in each against how often that country voted the same way as the United States in the UN General Assembly. They report that moving a country from never voting with the United States to always voting with it reduces the number of conditions by about three. They also report more conditions before elections for countries not voting with the United States, and fewer for closer allies, and they say that result "is not very robust" because it goes insignificant when the interaction term is included. They leave conditions broken down by sector and by type of condition "for future research", so neither study counts structural benchmarks separately.
entries.implications: If it holds, a condition is partly a price set by the largest members rather than a remedy drawn from the borrower's accounts, and two loans with the same economic numbers can carry different conditions. It would also mean that the thresholds in the Articles are not only about amendments: a member that can block a quota change can also make its views expensive to ignore in an ordinary programme discussion. For this map it would mean that the conditions recorded on a case are evidence about the lender's largest members as well as about the borrower.
entries.missing: No case on this map has had its conditions matched against the borrower's UN voting record or against what the largest members asked for. The two studies stop in 2003 and 2014, so nothing covers the programmes of the last decade. The Executive Board's own discussion of a programme is not on the map in any form. The documented pattern on aid that rises and falls with votes at the UN measures aid volumes, not the conditions attached to a loan, so it does not cover this.
entries.would_settle: Three published records read side by side for a run of programme approvals: the letters of intent and staff reports, which carry the conditions; the United States Treasury's annual report to Congress on the international financial institutions, which records how the US Executive Director voted and what policies it pressed for; and the IMF documents released under its archives policy once the waiting period has passed. Matching those votes and requests case by case against the conditions would show whether the two move together.

story: A country that has run out of money goes to the IMF or the World Bank and comes away with a list of things it must do before the money arrives: raise this tax, end that subsidy, sell that state company. The list is presented as arithmetic done on the country's own accounts. But both institutions are owned by their member governments, and members do not get a vote each. They get votes in proportion to the money they have paid in. What is probably true, and what nobody has shown programme by programme, is that part of what lands on the list is a price set by the largest shareholders, so two countries with the same broken accounts can be handed different lists.

The shareholdings are published. The IBRD's subscription table, with data as of 30 June 2026, gives 2,918,202 votes across 189 countries, of which the United States holds 466,319, or 15.98 per cent. The next largest holding is Japan's, at 6.88 per cent. At the IMF, as of 30 April 2025, the American share is 16.49 per cent. Those numbers matter because of a threshold in the IMF's Articles of Agreement, where 22 kinds of decision need eighty-five per cent of the total voting power. Worth doing slowly: if a decision needs eighty-five per cent, anybody holding more than fifteen per cent can stop it, because 100 minus 85 leaves 15. One member is above that line in both institutions.

What goes on the list has been counted. Three researchers reading 4,590 loan documents from 1985 to 2014 pulled out 55,465 individual conditions across 131 countries. A separate pair, working in 2003, took 206 letters of intent from 38 countries signed between April 1997 and February 2003 and set the number of conditions in each against how often that country had voted with the United States at the UN General Assembly. Moving a country from never voting with the United States to always voting with it, they report, takes about three conditions off its list. They are careful with their own result: a related finding about election years, they write, “is not very robust”.

It stays a suspicion because the room where the asking happens is shut. The Executive Board's discussion of a country's programme is not published, so no record shows which member pressed for what. Three published sets of papers would close that gap: the letters of intent and staff reports, which carry the conditions; the United States Treasury's annual report to Congress on the international financial institutions, which records how its Executive Director voted and what it pushed for; and the IMF papers released from the archives once the waiting period has run. Matched programme by programme, they would show whether conditions and votes move together. Nobody has tried it on the cases here, including the December 2001 Argentine card, where the Fund had raised its commitment to as much as US$22 billion and then cut support off.

entries.title: A small circle of arbitrators decides most of the claims companies bring against states
entries.conviction: One 2012 count over 450 cases by two campaign groups, and one register's own figures for 2025. The 2012 count has never been redone against the 1,332 cases now listed.
entries.summary:
UNCTAD's dispute settlement register lists 1,332 known investor-state claims, and its country table lists 146 countries. The tribunals that decide them are appointed case by case, usually three arbitrators, and there is no fixed bench.

In 2012 the Transnational Institute and Corporate Europe Observatory, two campaign organisations, counted who had sat on them. The count is theirs, not the register's. Of 450 investment-treaty disputes known at that date, they found 15 arbitrators had decided 247, which is 55 per cent. On the larger claims the share they report is higher: 79 of 123 disputes of at least US$100 million, 64 per cent, and 12 of 16 disputes of at least US$4 billion, 75 per cent. The same report counted three law firms, Freshfields, White & Case and King & Spalding, claiming involvement in 130 investment-treaty cases in 2011 alone. It also quotes one of the arbitrators it names saying that the existence of an elite group is an "illusion".

Repeat appointment is visible in the one register that publishes its own figures. ICSID had 1,085 cases registered under its Convention and Additional Facility rules as of 31 December 2025. In 2025 it recorded 240 appointments of arbitrators, conciliators and ad hoc committee members, covering 49 nationalities, and 13 per cent of those appointments were of someone sitting on an ICSID case for the first time. Nationals of Western European countries took 38 per cent of the 2025 appointments, the largest single regional group, and South American nationals 20 per cent. Women took 30 per cent of the 2025 appointments against 16 per cent across all cases historically.
entries.implications: If the concentration still holds across all 1,332 claims, then what a treaty means in practice is settled by a group small enough to know each other, and a state facing a claim is facing people who will hear the next one too. It would also mean that a reform aimed at treaty text leaves the deciding unchanged, because the same people would read the new text. For this map it would mean the arbitration cases on the cards are not separate events but repeat appearances.
entries.missing: Nobody has recounted the 2012 figure. UNCTAD's register names the arbitrators in most cases and ICSID publishes its tribunals, but no count by arbitrator across the 1,332 claims has been made here. An existing suspected pattern on this map counts 4 of its cases against those 1,332 claims; the ten cards listed below are the ones whose own text records a claim, which is a different and looser test. Either way this map's own cases are far too few to count anything from.
entries.would_settle: A full count of arbitrator names from the UNCTAD register and the ICSID case list, both of which are public, broken down by who appointed each one and by the size of the claim, repeating the 2012 method on the current caseload.

story: When a company decides a country has wronged it — a cancelled contract, a refused mining permit, a new environmental rule — it does not have to sue in that country's courts. Thousands of investment treaties let it bring the state before a private tribunal instead, and UNCTAD's register lists 1,332 such claims from 146 countries. There is no standing court and no permanent bench. Each tribunal is three arbitrators assembled for that one case: one chosen by the company, one by the state, one agreed between them. The probable position is that the pool those appointments come from is small enough that the same few people decide most of what the treaties turn out to mean.

Somebody has counted, once. In 2012 two campaign organisations, the Transnational Institute and Corporate Europe Observatory, went through the 450 investment-treaty disputes known at the time and worked out who had sat on them; the count is theirs, not the register's. Fifteen arbitrators had decided 247 of the 450, which is 55 per cent. The bigger the money, the tighter the circle: 79 of the 123 disputes worth at least US$100 million, and 12 of the 16 worth at least US$4 billion. One of the arbitrators the report names dismissed the idea of an elite group as an “illusion”. The one register that publishes figures on its own appointments points the same way: of the 240 appointments ICSID recorded during 2025, only 13 per cent went to someone sitting on an ICSID case for the first time.

Nobody has recounted it since, and the caseload has roughly tripled. If the concentration held, then what a treaty means in practice is settled by a group small enough to know one another, and a state defending a claim is arguing in front of people who will hear the next one. Rewriting treaty text would change less than it appears to, because the same readers would be reading the new words.

Settling this needs no new sources at all. The arbitrators are named in most of UNCTAD's entries and ICSID publishes its tribunals, so the 2012 method can simply be run again across all 1,332 claims, sorted by who appointed each arbitrator and by the size of the claim. The ten cases listed below are the ones whose own text records a claim — Cochabamba's water concession, Roșia Montană, Santurbán, Santa Ana, La Oroya. They are here to show what such a claim looks like where it lands, and they are far too few to count anything from.

entries.title: Once a country is in one bank's index, its own figures stop predicting whether it can borrow
entries.conviction: One journal article covering 60 developing countries from 1990 to 2015, one regulator's market-share table for 2024, and one UN agency's estimate. No test against this map's cases.
entries.summary:
Much of the money that buys a developing country's dollar bonds is not choosing that country. It is tracking an index. Cormier and Naqvi, in the Journal of Politics, studied inclusion in JP Morgan's Emerging Market Bond Index Global for 60 developing countries from 1990 to 2015. They report a World Bank estimate, from Raddatz, Schmukler and Williams, that 70 per cent of mutual fund investments and over 50 per cent of active portfolio investments in this market are explained by the composition of that one index. At least US$306 billion of assets formally tracked it in 2018, on JP Morgan's own figure. Its country coverage went from 14 countries at its creation in 1993 to 38 at the end of 2007 and 72 by January 2019.

Their finding is about what inclusion does to the borrower's own numbers. For countries left out of the index, or given very low weights, debt levels, fiscal deficits, the size of the economy and which party is in government have the effects on bond market access that would be expected. For countries inside the index with higher weights, those same features are unrelated to bond market access.

The criteria are not discretionary, and the paper says so: inclusion rests on a limited set of quantitative criteria set by JP Morgan, income per head below a ceiling, a credit rating below an investment-grade ceiling and bonds of at least US$500 million, and there is no lower bound for credit ratings. The paper calls these objective quantitative criteria and says they set this index apart from others. One of the criteria is a rating, and ratings come from a small number of firms. The European regulator's own market-share table for 2024, which measures turnover from rating activity among firms registered in the European Union, puts S&P Global Ratings Europe at 47.81 per cent, Moody's Investors Service at 30.59 per cent and Fitch Ratings Ireland at 11.86 per cent; added together here, 47.81 plus 30.59 plus 11.86 is 90.26 per cent of that registered market. The table covers the European Union only. The UNDP estimates that African countries "could save up to US$ 74.5 billion if credit ratings were based on less subjective assessments", in a study released on 17 April 2023.
entries.implications: If it holds, then whether a country can borrow privately turns on a threshold in one bank's rulebook and on a rating from one of three firms, not on what the country's own accounts say and not on any public decision. It would also mean that a country can do everything its lenders asked and still lose access because a threshold moved. For this map it would mean that the defaults and payment crises on the cards have an earlier step that no card records.
entries.missing: No case on this map has had the dates of its index inclusion or exclusion, or its rating actions, set against the dates money arrived or left. The index study ends in 2015 and the market-share table covers the European Union only, not the world. Nobody has checked whether the stated criteria were applied as written in any single inclusion or exclusion.
entries.would_settle: JP Morgan's published index rules and the monthly index composition going back far enough to date every entry and exit, set against the rating agencies' published sovereign rating actions and dated capital flow figures for the same countries. All three are published records.

entries.looked_at: One journal article on index inclusion, the European regulator's 2024 market-share calculation, and the UNDP's 2023 press statement of its Africa ratings study.
story: A government that wants to borrow from private lenders rather than from the IMF sells bonds, and the usual account of who buys them is that investors study the country: its debts, its deficit, the size of its economy, who won the last election. For much of this market that account is wrong. A great deal of the money is not choosing countries at all. It is tracking an index — a list kept by one investment bank — and buying what is on the list in the proportions the list sets. The probable consequence, measured once and not since, is that a country inside the index stops being judged on its own figures.

Cormier and Naqvi, in the Journal of Politics, studied membership of JP Morgan's Emerging Market Bond Index Global across 60 developing countries from 1990 to 2015. They cite a World Bank estimate that the make-up of that one list explains 70 per cent of mutual fund investment in this market, and JP Morgan's own figure that at least US$306 billion of assets formally tracked it in 2018. The list has grown from 14 countries at its creation in 1993 to 72 by January 2019. Their finding is the odd part. For countries left out of the index, or holding very low weights in it, debt levels, deficits, the size of the economy and which party governs affect access to the bond market in the directions anyone would predict. For countries inside it at higher weights, those same things bear no relation to access at all.

Membership is not decided behind a closed door, and the paper is explicit about that: the tests are published and quantitative — income per head under a ceiling, a credit rating below an investment-grade ceiling, bonds worth at least US$500 million. Follow one of them, though, and it leads somewhere narrow. A rating is a condition of entry, and ratings come from very few firms: three of them account for 90.26 per cent of turnover from rating work among firms registered in the European Union, on the European regulator's own 2024 figures. The UNDP put a price on the judgement involved, estimating in April 2023 that African countries “could save up to US$ 74.5 billion if credit ratings were based on less subjective assessments”.

Put together, that would mean a country can do everything its lenders asked and still lose access to money because a threshold moved in a rulebook it does not own. Zambia's 2020 Eurobond default is on this map, with private lenders refusing a payment suspension, and so is Sri Lanka's missed payment in 2022. Neither card records the rating actions or the index treatment that came before it, and Ghana appears in 16 cases here without one of them mentioning either. The records needed are public: JP Morgan's index rules and monthly composition, going back far enough to date every entry and exit, set against the agencies' published sovereign rating actions and dated capital flow figures. Nobody has yet checked whether the stated tests were applied as written in even one case.

entries.title: Rules made by bodies whose decisions have no legal force are written into national law, and one body's list is followed by a fall in capital inflows
entries.conviction: One standard-setter's own charter and one IMF working paper covering 89 countries. The listings have not been matched against anything on this map.
entries.summary:
Some of the rules that decide whether money can cross a border are written by bodies that make no law. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision says so in its own charter: "The BCBS does not possess any formal supranational authority" and "Its decisions do not have legal force." The same charter says it "relies on its members' commitments" instead, that it "expects full implementation of its standards by BCBS members and their internationally active banks", and that it expects its standards written into local legal frameworks "within the pre-defined timeframe established by the Committee". It also says its standards are minimum requirements and that members may go beyond them.

The measured version of the effect belongs to a different body. An IMF working paper by Mizuho Kida and Simon Paetzold, whose views the IMF says are the authors' own, studied capital flows in 89 emerging and developing countries over 2000 to 2017 and found that being placed on the Financial Action Task Force's grey list cuts a country's capital inflows by 7.6 per cent of GDP on average. The paper says its result holds "despite the small number of gray-listings in the sample". It is less confident about the literature it sits in: "the empirical evidence for these effects is weak. There have only been a few studies, some of which found little or no effect." It summarises five of them. Kudrle in 2009 found little systematic effect on cross-border bank flows in 38 tax havens. Balakina, D'Andrea and Masciandaro in 2016 found no consistent effect on bank flows in 126 countries. Collin, Cook and Soramaki in 2016, using SWIFT records of cross-border payments from 2004 to 2014, found listing cut the number of payments sent to a listed country by 7 to 10 per cent, but found no consistent effect on payments sent from it and none on payments between listed countries.

The listing process is set out in the same paper's appendix. The task force was established in 1989 by the G-7 and is described there as an intergovernmental body. It has issued 40 recommendations and has published lists since 2000. Countries are assessed by the task force, by nine regional bodies and occasionally by the IMF or World Bank; reports are adopted at plenary meetings where "evaluated countries may argue against portions of the draft report or advocate rating changes"; and a country goes on the grey list once an action plan is adopted by the task force and committed to by the country. When the paper was written 19 countries were on the grey list and two, Iran and North Korea, on the list for which the task force calls on others to act. The mechanism it describes for the effect is banks ending relationships to cut compliance costs, and investors treating a listing as a shorthand for risk.
entries.implications: If it holds, a decision taken in a body that makes no law can do more to a country's access to money than any loan condition, and the rules a borrower has to meet are not only the ones in its loan agreement. For this map it would mean that a card describing a country's loss of access may be describing a listing or a bank withdrawal rather than a lending decision. The effect size, 7.6 per cent of GDP, is larger than most of the loan amounts on this map.
entries.missing: Nobody has set grey-listing dates against the cases on this map. Of the 19 countries on the grey list named in the paper, 17 have at least one case here, 175 cases between them when last counted, before round 22 added cases, counted from the cases' own country codes. No card on this map mentions the task force or grey-listing at all, and a text search of the cards finds only three that mention correspondent banking, which is a floor and not a measurement, because the search finds only cards whose text already says the words. The Basel Committee's published jurisdictional assessments have not been read, and the two bodies have not been shown to work the same way: one expects its standards in national law, the other lists countries.
entries.would_settle: Three published sets of records. The task force's own mutual evaluation reports and the action plans agreed with listed countries, which are published, set against dated capital flow and bank exposure figures for the months either side of each listing. And the Basel Committee's published assessments of each member jurisdiction, which record whether and when its standards entered national law.

story: Two of the committees that decide whether money can cross a border hold no legal power at all, and say so themselves. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision writes in its own charter that it has no formal supranational authority and that “Its decisions do not have legal force.” What it has instead is its members' commitments: it expects them and their internationally active banks to apply its standards in full, and expects those standards written into national law within a timetable it sets itself. The probable position is that rules made this way reach further into a country than any loan condition does, without ever passing through a parliament.

The measured version of the effect belongs to the other body. An IMF working paper by Mizuho Kida and Simon Paetzold, whose views the Fund notes are the authors' own, tracked capital flows in 89 emerging and developing countries from 2000 to 2017 and found that being placed on the Financial Action Task Force's grey list cuts the money coming into a country by 7.6 per cent of its GDP on average. The authors say that holds even though few countries in their sample were ever listed, and they are blunt about the field around them: the evidence for these effects, they write, is weak. Of the five earlier studies they summarise, two found no consistent effect on bank flows at all.

Getting on that list is a committee decision. The task force was set up by the G-7 in 1989 and has published lists since 2000. Countries are assessed by it, by nine regional bodies and sometimes by the IMF or World Bank, and the reports are adopted at plenary meetings where the country under assessment may argue against parts of the draft or press for a different rating. A country joins the grey list once it has agreed an action plan; 19 were on it when the paper was written. The damage then travels through ordinary commercial caution, as banks drop relationships rather than carry the compliance cost and investors read a listing as shorthand for risk.

The figure to sit with is 7.6 per cent of GDP, which is larger than most of the loans recorded on this map. Seventeen of those 19 listed countries have at least one case here, 175 between them, counted from the cases' own country codes — Pakistan 29, Uganda 24, Myanmar 20, Ghana 16. Not one card mentions the task force or a listing. Settling it means setting listing dates against dated capital flow and bank exposure figures for the months either side, out of the task force's own published evaluations and action plans. The Basel half needs separate work: the committee publishes an assessment of each member jurisdiction recording whether and when its standards entered national law, and nobody here has read them. The two bodies have not been shown to work alike, and one entry covering both is doing that join on an assumption.

entries.title: Loans repaid in oil and minerals are signed on terms that are almost never published
entries.conviction: One counted dataset of 52 loans, whose authors say it is incomplete and may not be representative.
entries.summary:
A state short of money can borrow against oil or minerals it has not produced yet. The Natural Resource Governance Institute counted the deals it could find: 52 resource-backed loans signed between 2004 and 2018 in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America, agreed by 14 countries, worth US$164 billion, of which US$66 billion was taken by sub-Saharan African countries and US$98 billion by Latin American ones. Thirty of the 52 were agreed by African countries and 22 by Latin American ones. Chinese policy banks were the lender in 38 of the 52. Commodity traders were the lender in seven, Chinese state-owned enterprises in four, and the Export-Import Bank of Korea, the Nigerian government and Rosneft in one each. Forty-three of the 52 were backed by oil, six by minerals, two by cocoa and one by tobacco.

The figure that makes this a suspected pattern rather than a finding is a disclosure count. The report says the loan agreements "are only available in one out of the 52 cases, the Sicomines deal in the DRC", and that the loans it identified from public sources "are all missing key pieces of information". It is not a total blackout: summary documents were published on their own in Ghana and inside a bond prospectus in Angola, and basic information such as the interest rate could be identified for 19 of the 52. On oil advances the report says commodity traders "are just as opaque as other lenders" and generally make substantial disclosures only when repayment problems emerge. It notes that traders bring banks in behind them, and gives Deutsche Bank, Credit Agricole and ING partly financing Glencore's loan to Chad as its example.

This map already documents the Chinese state version of a nearby shape in the pattern on secrecy and security in Chinese loan contracts, where 100 contracts were published and found to carry confidentiality clauses and lender-controlled revenue accounts. Those are 100 contracts from a different dataset. For loans repaid in output there is one published agreement in 52.
entries.implications: If it holds, a share of a country's future export earnings is committed under terms no citizen, parliament or other creditor can read, and the lender may be a trading company rather than a bank or a state. It would also mean that a country's published debt figures understate what is owed, because an advance against future cargoes may not appear as debt. For this map it would mean that the austerity and seizure cases in oil-exporting countries have a contract behind them that cannot be obtained.
entries.missing: The map holds no case where an advance against future output is the mechanism on the card. The dataset stops in 2018, and the report says it "is by no means comprehensive" and that it cannot be sure the sample is representative or the terms accurate. Thirty-eight of the 52 loans are from Chinese policy banks, so most of the dataset sits inside the ground already covered by the documented pattern on Chinese loan contracts; the part that is not covered is the seven trader loans and the disclosure rate across all lenders. Nobody has looked at the debt registers of the 14 countries to see which advances they list.
entries.would_settle: The borrowing states' published debt registers and debt management office reports, listing each advance with its interest rate, maturity, security and the volume of output pledged, counted against the 52 deals to see how many appear in official debt figures at all.

countries.note: The card on debt funds records a Houston court issuing garnishment orders in 2006 on more than 500,000 barrels, which an ECB study says blocked Congo from receiving royalties or export revenue from that oil, and the High Court finding that Congo sold oil through prepayment deals 'very expensive for SNPC' partly to avoid seizure. The NRGI report records Congo releasing extra information on its advances in late 2018 alongside an IMF programme.

countries.note: The report says Angola received the largest amount of these loans in sub-Saharan Africa, with Chinese lenders committing over US$24 billion of oil-backed loans and credit lines between 2000 and 2016, and that a summary document appeared in a bond prospectus. The map's four Angolan cases are fuel protests and projects, none about the loans.

entries.looked_at: The NRGI report Resource-Backed Loans: Pitfalls and Potential, including its dataset description, its figures by lender and commodity, and its section on hidden terms.
story: A government short of cash can borrow against oil or copper it has not dug up yet, promising future cargoes instead of future tax revenue. The lender gets repaid in barrels or tonnes, or out of an account the cargoes are sold into. The probable position, and the reason this sits here rather than among the findings, is that almost nobody outside the two signing parties ever sees what was promised — not the country's parliament, not its other creditors, not the people whose oil it is.

The Natural Resource Governance Institute went looking for these deals and found 52 of them, signed between 2004 and 2018 by 14 countries in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America, worth US$164 billion together. Chinese policy banks were the lender in 38. Commodity traders were the lender in seven more, and traders bring banks in behind them: Deutsche Bank, Crédit Agricole and ING each helped finance Glencore's loan to Chad. Forty-three of the 52 were backed by oil, six by minerals, two by cocoa and one by tobacco. Then the disclosure count, which is the whole reason this is a suspicion and not a finding: of those 52 loan agreements, the researchers could obtain exactly one, the Sicomines deal in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is not a complete blackout. Summary documents surfaced on their own in Ghana and inside a bond prospectus in Angola, and something as basic as the interest rate could be established for 19 of the 52. The rest is inference from public traces.

Two things follow that a reader should not have to assemble alone. First, a slice of a country's future export earnings can be committed without any voter, legislator or rival creditor being able to read the terms. Second, an advance against cargoes may not be recorded as debt at all, which means the published debt figures of these countries can be too low by an unknown amount. The report is careful about its own limits, saying its dataset is not comprehensive and that it cannot be certain the sample is representative or the terms accurate.

This map already documents the nearby Chinese version, where 100 published loan contracts were found carrying confidentiality clauses and revenue accounts the lender controls. Those are 100 contracts from a different dataset; for loans repaid in output, it is one agreement in 52. What the map does not hold is a single case where an advance against future production is the mechanism on the card, though the consequences are here: a Houston court issued garnishment orders in 2006 over more than 500,000 barrels of Congolese oil, and the High Court later found Congo-Brazzaville had been selling oil through prepayment deals that were expensive for its own state company, partly to keep the cargoes out of creditors' reach. The test is dull and available. The 14 borrowing states publish debt registers and debt management office reports; counting how many of the 52 advances appear in them at all, with their interest rate, maturity, security and the volume of output pledged, would show whether this money is being recorded as debt or kept off the books.

entries.title: About half of one development lender's long-term commitments go through banks, and the end borrower is not named
entries.conviction: One compliance audit and one campaign report, both about the International Finance Corporation alone, and both at least nine years old.
entries.summary:
A development lender can lend to a project or it can lend to a bank that lends to projects. The second kind leaves no public record of where the money ended up. The Compliance Advisor Ombudsman's audit of 10 October 2012 found that financial-market activities "constitute over 40 percent of IFC's portfolio, and the proportion has been growing." The same audit found that "the absence of any systematic measurement of impacts or outcomes at the subclient level means that IFC is unable to measure the actual effectiveness" of the management system it requires of the bank, and that potential complainants "may not know about IFC's relationship to the subclient transaction - or about the CAO as an available recourse mechanism." It took a 10 per cent sample of 737 projects, 74 in all, and said the sample "is in no way statistically representative". It also found that clients already interested in these issues often used the required system to manage, and sometimes to improve, the outcomes of their lending.

Inclusive Development International, a campaign organisation, counted the same portfolio in 2016. It found long-term investments in financial intermediaries up 45 per cent between the 2010 and 2015 financial years and making up approximately 50 per cent of long-term commitments in 2015, a figure that excludes short-term trade finance. In that year the lender put US$507 million into funds and more than US$4.5 billion into financial markets. From those two figures the report concludes that the lender "considers itself to have little responsibility for the end use of around 90 percent of its FI business". That conclusion is the campaign organisation's, drawn from the lender's own answer to it, which was that "IFC does not finance specific companies through its investments in FIs, except in the case of Private Equity Funds" and that most of its clients' investments are therefore outside its direct supervision. Private equity funds, the part whose investments are disclosed, were 6 per cent of the whole intermediary portfolio including short-term trade finance, and 10 per cent counting long-term investments only.

Two cards on this map reach a sub-client. One records a palm oil and plantation group identified through its bank financiers; the other records coal plants financed through a bank. Both were found by someone tracing the chain backwards, not from any published list.
entries.implications: If it holds, then for roughly half of one lender's long-term money there is no list of the projects it paid for, and a person harmed by one of them has no way of knowing a development lender is behind it. It would also mean that the complaint registers this map relies on cannot cover that half, because a complaint requires knowing who financed you. For this map it would put a floor under the thinness noted in the suspected pattern on missing registers: for intermediary lending there is no list to work from at all.
entries.missing: Both sources are about one lender, and the newer is from 2016. The current share of intermediary lending has not been counted, and no equivalent count has been made for the other development lenders, the regional banks or the bilateral development finance institutions. Nobody has counted how many of this map's cases were financed through an intermediary rather than directly.
entries.would_settle: The lender's published project disclosure for one financial year, counting how many intermediary sub-projects are named there against the number of intermediary commitments in that year's annual report. Repeating the count for two or three other development lenders would show whether the share is general.

countries.role: Sub-client reached by tracing the financiers
countries.note: The Indofood and London Sumatra card names the banks behind the group. It exists because someone traced the chain, not because a list was published.

entries.looked_at: The CAO's 2012 compliance audit of IFC investments in third-party financial intermediaries, and Inclusive Development International's 2016 report on the same portfolio.
story: A development lender can put money into a project, in which case the project has a name, a location and a published document. Or it can put the money into a commercial bank or a fund and let that institution lend it onward. The second kind leaves no public record of where the money ended up. The probable position is that for roughly half of one such lender's long-term money, no list exists anywhere of what it paid for, which means a person whose land or water was ruined by one of those projects has no way of discovering that a development bank financed it.

The lender is the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank Group's private-sector arm, and the first count is its own watchdog's. In an audit dated 10 October 2012 the Compliance Advisor Ombudsman found that financial-market activities made up over 40 per cent of the corporation's portfolio and that the share was growing. The audit's central finding was about not knowing: because nothing systematically measures what happens at the level of the bank's own borrowers, the corporation cannot tell whether the environmental and social system it requires of those banks works at all. It also noted that someone harmed may simply not know the corporation is connected to the transaction, and therefore not know the complaints office exists. The auditors looked at 74 projects, a tenth of 737, and said plainly that the sample was in no way statistically representative.

Inclusive Development International, a campaign organisation, counted the same portfolio in 2016 and found long-term investment in these intermediaries up 45 per cent between the 2010 and 2015 financial years, reaching about half of all long-term commitments by 2015. In that year the corporation put US$507 million into funds and more than US$4.5 billion into financial markets. The organisation's reading of the corporation's own reply to it — that it does not finance specific companies through these investments except in private equity funds — was that the lender treats itself as having little responsibility for the end use of around 90 per cent of this business. That conclusion is theirs. The disclosed slice, private equity funds, was 6 per cent of the whole intermediary portfolio.

Two cards on this map got through to a sub-client, and both only because a person traced the chain backwards from the harm: a palm oil and plantation group in Indonesia identified through the banks funding it, and coal plants in the Philippines reached through a bank rather than a direct loan. Neither came off a published list, because there is no published list. This also puts a floor under a problem noted elsewhere on this map, that the complaint registers it relies on cannot cover intermediary lending — filing a complaint requires knowing who financed you. Both sources here are about one lender and the newer is from 2016, so the first thing to do is simple: take one financial year, count how many intermediary sub-projects are named in the lender's published disclosure against the number of intermediary commitments in that year's annual report, then repeat it for two or three other development banks.

entries.title: Donors pay for the preparation inside a development bank, and three-quarters of what they give its own trust funds is tied to a named country
entries.conviction: The lender's own trust fund report for one year, read once. No test of whether the earmarking changed what was prepared.
entries.summary:
Alongside its own capital, a development lender holds money that donors give it to spend. The World Bank Group's trust fund annual report for the 2024 financial year records US$17.8 billion of contributions to its trust funds and financial intermediary funds in that year, and US$35.1 billion in 2023. Of those two kinds of fund, the earmarking figures below are about the Bank's own IBRD and IDA trust funds only, not the intermediary funds, whose contributions over the same five years were 99 per cent for global purposes, US$51.6 billion.

For the IBRD and IDA trust funds the report gives five-year figures. Over the 2020 to 2024 financial years, sovereign governments provided 91 per cent of the cash contributions, US$37.8 billion. The United States was the largest single contributor at US$24.1 billion, then Germany at US$2.3 billion and the United Kingdom at US$2.0 billion. US$23.1 billion of the United States' US$24.1 billion was for trust funds supporting Ukraine. Of those contributions, 76 per cent, US$31.5 billion, was for country-specific purposes, which the report says were "primarily to support Ukraine, Afghanistan, Ethiopia, and West Bank and Gaza"; 21 per cent, US$8.5 billion, was for global purposes and 3 per cent, US$1.4 billion, regional or other.

Part of the money is spent by the Bank itself rather than passed to a recipient. The report calls these Bank-executed activities and defines them as work done directly by the Bank Group "including advisory services and analytics, research and knowledge products, technical assistance and capacity building, and project preparation and supervision". Bank-executed disbursing accounts paid out US$1.3 billion in the 2024 financial year. Advisory services and analytics paid for from these accounts were US$0.5 billion in each of the 2020 and 2021 financial years, US$0.6 billion in 2022 and US$0.7 billion in each of 2023 and 2024, across a project count that fell from 2,453 to 1,783. Trust funds supported 11 per cent of total World Bank disbursements for recipient-executed activities over the same five years. The largest umbrella programme by disbursement over the five years was the Afghanistan Resilience Trust Fund, at US$2.8 billion.

The terms are the part that is not published. The Bank publishes totals by donor and by country type. The individual administration agreements, which say what a donor's money may and may not be used for, are not published alongside them.
entries.implications: If it holds, then part of the choice of what gets studied and prepared is a donor's choice rather than the lender's, and a country with no donor interested in it gets no preparatory work, however large its need. It would also mean the figures a lender publishes about its own priorities describe money it did not direct.
entries.missing: Only one year's report has been read, and the figures are totals rather than a breakdown by activity. No administration agreement has been obtained. Nobody has checked whether the countries that received Bank-executed trust fund money went on to receive more lending than comparable countries that did not. The documented pattern on earmarked multilateral money states in its own uncertainty note that no figure was found for how much of the money given to development banks is earmarked, so this is the figure that pattern says it lacks, rather than a repeat of it; the documented pattern on tied aid is about which companies win contracts, which is a different question.
entries.would_settle: The published list of advisory and analytical work paid for from Bank-executed trust funds, by country and year, set against the Bank's published lending commitments by country for the years that followed. Both are published; the comparison has not been made.

entries.looked_at: The World Bank Group trust fund annual report covering the 2024 financial year: its Table 2, its figures 9, 11, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 20, and its glossary.
story: Before a loan exists, somebody has to study the country, write the analysis and prepare the project. That work decides what is ever proposed, and it is paid for separately. Alongside its own capital, the World Bank Group holds money that donor governments give it to spend, and three-quarters of what goes into the Bank's own trust funds arrives earmarked for a named country. The probable consequence is that part of the choice of what gets studied and prepared belongs to donors rather than to the lender, so a country with no donor interested in it gets no preparatory work however badly it needs some.

The figures are the Bank's own, from its trust fund report for the 2024 financial year. Contributions that year came to US$17.8 billion, and US$35.1 billion the year before. Over the five years to 2024, governments supplied 91 per cent of the cash going into the IBRD and IDA trust funds, US$37.8 billion. The United States was the largest single contributor at US$24.1 billion, and US$23.1 billion of that — almost all of it — was for trust funds supporting Ukraine. Germany gave US$2.3 billion and the United Kingdom US$2.0 billion. Of all those contributions, 76 per cent, or US$31.5 billion, was tied to particular countries, which the report says were mainly Ukraine, Afghanistan, Ethiopia and West Bank and Gaza. Just 21 per cent was for global purposes.

Some of this money never reaches a recipient government at all; the Bank spends it itself. The report calls that Bank-executed work and defines it as including advisory services, analytics, research, technical assistance, and project preparation and supervision — in other words, the groundwork. Those accounts paid out US$1.3 billion in the 2024 financial year, with advisory and analytical work rising from US$0.5 billion a year in 2020 to US$0.7 billion in 2024 while the number of projects it was spread across fell from 2,453 to 1,783.

What is not published is the part that would show whether the earmarking bites. The Bank publishes totals by donor and by country type, but not the individual administration agreements, which are the documents that say what a donor's money may and may not be used for. Only one year's report has been read for this entry and no agreement has been obtained. The comparison that would settle it uses two things the Bank already publishes: the list of advisory and analytical work paid for out of Bank-executed trust funds, by country and year, set against its lending commitments by country in the years that followed. If preparation paid for by a donor is followed by lending, the sequence is visible. Ukraine has eight cases on this map and Ethiopia fifteen, and not one of them records trust fund money.
